"I changed welfare, I changed quality of life, I took on homelessness -- I did all the things that they think makes you mean and I believe show true compassion and true love for people." "Mr. McCain was one of the first prominent Republicans to point out how badly the war in Iraq was being managed. We wish he could now see as clearly past the temporary victories produced by Mr. Bush's unsustainable escalation, which have not led to any change in Iraq's murderous political calculus," it reads. "At the least, he owes Americans a real idea of how he would win this war, which he says he can do." The paper praised Clinton's chief rival, Sen. Barack Obama, but called Clinton more qualified for the job. "It is unfair, especially after seven years of Mr. Bush's inept leadership, but any Democrat will face tougher questioning about his or her fitness to be commander in chief," it reads. "Mrs. Clinton has more than cleared that bar, using her years in the Senate well to immerse herself in national security issues, and has won the respect of world leaders and many in the American military." The Democratic editorial contrasts Clinton and Obama -- calling her "the brilliant if at times harsh-sounding senator from New York" and him "the incandescent if still undefined senator from Illinois." The paper says Clinton "sometimes overstates the importance of [her] resume," but that upon hearing "her policies and answers for America's big problems, we are hugely impressed by the depth of her knowledge, by the force of her intellect and by the breadth of, yes, her experience." NEW YORK (CNN) — The New York Times backed Arizona Senator John McCain for the Republican presidential nomination, choosing him over Rudy Giuliani and the other GOP contenders while delivering a particularly severe assessment of the former New York City mayor.

McCain and Giuliani participated in a Republican debate in Florida on Thursday. In endorsements published online for its Friday editions, the Times also supported New York Senator Hillary Clinton for the Democratic nomination.

The newspaper’s editorial board argued that McCain was the only Republican candidate offering a clear break from President George W. Bush’s approach to governing, which it characterized as serving a small and resentful faction. It also pointed to McCain’s history of cooperating with Democrats on bipartisan legislation, saying that record could make him attractive to a wider segment of the electorate than his Republican rivals.

The editorial acknowledged that readers might question why the New York-based paper was rejecting Giuliani. The Times had endorsed him for another term as mayor in 1997 and had commended both his efforts to reduce crime and his leadership during the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

However, the board maintained that the Giuliani it had once supported was no longer the person seeking the presidency. It accused the 2008 candidate of converting the tragedy of 9/11 into a profitable business with an undisclosed client roster, then using the trauma suffered by New York and the nation to advance his White House campaign. The editorial portrayed him as narrow-minded, intensely secretive and vindictive.

Giuliani dismissed the criticism, noting that the Times’ liberal editorial board had frequently opposed him. During an MSNBC-hosted Republican debate Thursday night in Boca Raton, Florida, he said he had probably ignored the paper’s recommendations throughout his eight years as mayor and suggested that following its advice would have prevented him from being regarded as a conservative Republican.

He cited his record on welfare reform, quality-of-life concerns and homelessness, saying the Times viewed such policies as cruel while he considered them evidence of genuine compassion and concern for people.

Other Republican campaigns responded similarly. An e-mail from former Massachusetts Governor Mitt Romney’s campaign sarcastically referred to the Times, which had endorsed McCain, as a leading center of conservative advocacy.

Although the newspaper chose McCain, its editorial also included significant criticism. It described him as an authentic war hero and a committed supporter of campaign-finance reform, but challenged his position on Iraq.

The Times noted that McCain had been among the earliest prominent Republicans to recognize how poorly the Iraq War was being managed. Nevertheless, it said he was failing to look beyond the short-term gains associated with Bush’s troop escalation, which the board considered unsustainable and said had not altered Iraq’s deadly political dynamics. At a minimum, the editorial argued, McCain needed to give Americans a credible explanation of how he intended to achieve the victory he claimed was possible.

On the Democratic side, the paper complimented Senator Barack Obama but concluded that Clinton had stronger qualifications for the presidency.

The editorial said Democratic candidates would likely receive more intense scrutiny over their readiness to serve as commander in chief, even though that standard seemed unfair after seven years of what it called Bush’s incompetent leadership. It argued that Clinton had more than met the requirement by using her Senate tenure to gain a deep understanding of national-security matters and by earning the regard of international leaders and many members of the U.S. military.

In comparing the two candidates, the Times depicted Clinton as highly intelligent but occasionally severe in tone, while describing the Illinois senator as inspiring yet not fully defined.

The board also said Clinton sometimes exaggerated the value of her résumé. Even so, it expressed strong admiration for her command of policy and her proposed responses to major national challenges, citing the depth of her knowledge, the strength of her intellect and the wide scope of her experience.

New York was among the many states scheduled to hold primary voting on February 5, known as Super Tuesday. The original online article also included an option for readers to e-mail it to a friend.

# New York Times Backs Clinton and McCain in 2008 Presidential Primaries

**NEW YORK, Jan. 25, 2008** — The New York Times endorsed Senator Hillary Rodham Clinton of New York and Senator John McCain of Arizona in the 2008 Democratic and Republican presidential primaries, praising both candidates’ experience while delivering especially sharp criticism of McCain’s leading Republican rivals, Rudolph W. Giuliani and Mitt Romney.

The endorsements, published as the presidential nominating contests accelerated toward Florida’s Republican primary and the nationwide Super Tuesday vote, reflected markedly different assessments of the two parties’ fields. On the Democratic side, the newspaper described a difficult choice between two formidable candidates. In the Republican race, it portrayed McCain as the only acceptable option among the leading contenders.

## Clinton chosen over Obama

In endorsing Clinton, the Times said the Democratic contest offered voters two strong candidates: Clinton and Senator Barack Obama of Illinois. The editorial praised Obama’s political gifts and the historic nature of his candidacy, calling him the first African American with a viable opportunity to win a major party’s presidential nomination.

The newspaper nevertheless concluded that Clinton was better prepared to assume the presidency immediately. It cited her knowledge of domestic and international policy, her years in the Senate and her familiarity with the workings of the executive branch from her time as first lady.

The endorsement was not unqualified. The Times criticized aspects of Clinton’s campaign, including what it described as excessive calculation and a tendency to avoid taking clear political risks. It also raised concerns about former President Bill Clinton’s prominent and sometimes combative role in the campaign.

Still, the editorial said Clinton had shown resilience, intelligence and command of the issues. It argued that she had offered more detailed proposals on health care, the economy and other domestic matters and had demonstrated an ability to work within Washington’s political system.

Obama, the paper said, represented the possibility of a less polarized and more inspiring political era. But it questioned whether his relative lack of experience would allow him to deliver on that promise as effectively as Clinton could.

Former Senator John Edwards of North Carolina was credited with drawing attention to poverty, economic inequality and the struggles of working Americans. The newspaper, however, did not place him on the same level as Clinton and Obama in its assessment of readiness for the presidency.

## McCain endorsed as a rebuke to the Republican field

The Times’ Republican endorsement was more emphatic. It selected McCain as the candidate best positioned to move the country away from what the editorial described as the failures of President George W. Bush’s administration.

The newspaper praised McCain’s record on campaign-finance reform, immigration, torture and certain environmental issues. It also pointed to his willingness to challenge members of his own party and to work with Democrats.

At the same time, the editorial made clear that it disagreed with McCain on major questions. It criticized his support for the Iraq war and his opposition to abortion rights, and it expressed concern about some of his positions on taxes and judicial appointments. Nevertheless, it said he had displayed more independence, experience and integrity than the other Republican candidates.

The editorial was particularly severe toward Giuliani, the former New York City mayor whose presidential campaign had been built largely around his leadership after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. The Times had frequently clashed with Giuliani during his mayoralty and argued that his national campaign presented an incomplete and misleading portrait of his record.

It characterized Giuliani as secretive, vindictive and divisive, questioning both his temperament and his commitment to civil liberties. The paper also criticized his business relationships and his repeated use of Sept. 11 as the central rationale for his candidacy.

Romney, the former governor of Massachusetts, was faulted for changing positions as he moved from politics in a heavily Democratic state to a national Republican campaign. The Times contrasted Romney’s earlier positions on abortion rights, gun control and gay rights with the more conservative views he adopted while seeking the Republican nomination.

Former Arkansas Gov. Mike Huckabee received some credit for speaking about the economic concerns of working-class voters. But the newspaper criticized his positions on social issues and questioned his understanding of foreign affairs. It also concluded that former Senator Fred Thompson had failed to show the energy or commitment expected of a presidential candidate.

## Giuliani dismisses the criticism

Giuliani and his aides responded by portraying the endorsement as predictable hostility from a newspaper that had often criticized him.

Giuliani said he had not expected the Times’ support and suggested that an endorsement from the paper would have been of little value in a Republican primary. His campaign argued that the editorial board had long distorted his record as mayor and was fundamentally opposed to the policies that had made him popular with Republican voters.

Campaign representatives sought to turn the rejection into an asset, presenting it as evidence that Giuliani had stood up to one of the country’s most influential liberal institutions. The response was consistent with the former mayor’s broader campaign strategy of emphasizing his confrontations with political opponents and the New York press.

The endorsement came at a precarious moment for Giuliani. After largely bypassing Iowa, New Hampshire and other early contests, he had concentrated his resources on Florida. That strategy left him seeking to revive a campaign that had once led national Republican polls but had lost momentum as other candidates accumulated victories and delegates.

## Romney campaign calls McCain the liberal choice

Romney’s campaign likewise attempted to use the endorsement against McCain rather than treat it as a damaging judgment of Romney.

A Romney spokesman described the Times editorial board as a liberal institution and argued that it had selected the Republican candidate who most closely matched its own editorial views. The campaign’s message was that praise from the Times should make conservative voters suspicious of McCain.

The reaction fit Romney’s effort to cast himself as the reliable conservative in the race. His campaign had repeatedly attacked McCain for working with Democrats on immigration, campaign-finance restrictions and other legislation unpopular with parts of the Republican base.

McCain’s supporters, by contrast, treated the endorsement as further validation of his experience and independence. Although the Times’ approval could be politically complicated in a Republican primary, it reinforced McCain’s reputation as a candidate capable of attracting independents and voters beyond the party’s conservative core.

## Endorsements arrive at a pivotal point

The dual endorsements highlighted the unusual shape of the 2008 race. Democrats were deciding between Clinton’s argument for experience and Obama’s promise of generational and political change. Republicans were confronting divisions over ideology, immigration, national security and the legacy of the Bush administration.

For Clinton, the Times endorsement provided a valuable institutional boost in her home state and beyond, particularly as she and Obama prepared for a long series of delegate contests.

For McCain, the support came as he sought to consolidate moderate Republicans, independents and national-security voters. But the reactions from Giuliani and Romney also illustrated the risk: in a Republican primary, endorsement by a newspaper widely viewed as liberal could quickly become ammunition for conservative rivals.

The Times acknowledged those ideological differences but concluded that Clinton and McCain were the candidates best equipped to lead their respective parties—and, ultimately, the country.
